concepts: Authority to act in customer interactions
sections.description: Our friends at L.L. Bean have the same process around giving the front line the ability to work from their heart and their gut and make the decisions that they know are right.
sections.title: Frontline empowerment: heart and gut decisions

sections.description: Now I know you need to put some parameters around that, but start with believing.
sections.title: Begin with believing

sections.description: There's a reason why sorry is the last decision in the chapter of this book.
sections.title: Apology as last decision

sections.description: It's that you need to believe your people.
sections.title: Believe your people

sections.description: You need to be clear about the higher purpose you have with customers.
sections.title: higher purpose in customer care

sections.description: You need to be real and human. You need to be operationally deliberate to know where the breakdowns are happening.
sections.title: Real, human, and deliberate service

sections.description: And that enables the best kind of sorry that repairs the emotional connection.
sections.title: Emotional repair through apologizing

sections.description: As a result, they're worshipped and they just had annual sales of 1.5 billion dollars.
sections.title: Business impact: L.L. Bean example

summary: Jeanne Bliss presents a concise leadership approach that centers frontline empowerment: give frontline staff the authority to act from their heart and gut to make guiding decisions for customers. The talk emphasizes starting with belief in people, aligning actions with a clear higher purpose for customers, and maintaining real, human interactions while being operationally deliberate to identify where service breakdowns occur. The speaker argues that apologies should be the last resort, used to repair the emotional connection once the underlying issues are understood. The message is supported by a brief business example referencing L.L. Bean's performance, illustrating how customer-centric frontline behavior can correlate with strong company results, such as substantial annual sales (about 1.5 billion).
title: Can Your Frontline Rescue Customers?
